items.readable_text:
Content:
In this lesson, we'll learn how to construct confidence intervals for population proportions when the population we're sampling is finite. First, let's quickly recap some important results.

Content:
Suppose we have a random sample of size [MATH: n] from a sufficiently large population where a proportion [MATH: p] of the population has a particular characteristic. Then, we have the following approximation:

Content:
[MATH: \widehat{\,p} \sim N\left(p, \dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}\right)]
where [MATH: \widehat{\,p}] is the sample proportion. Now, if we [MATH: z]-score this result, we have

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{\widehat{\,p} - p}{\sqrt{\dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}}} \sim N(0,1).]

Content:
Replacing our expression for the variance with its sample-based estimate, we have

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{\widehat{\,p} - p}{\sqrt{\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})}{n}}\phantom{|}} \sim N(0,1).]

Content:
For this result to be valid, the following conditions must be satisfied:

Content:
- More than five members of the sample have the characteristic [MATH: (n \widehat{\,p} > 5),] and
- More than five members of the sample do not have the characteristic [MATH: (n (1-\widehat{\,p}) > 5).]

Content:
Then, for a given value [MATH: \alpha] between [MATH: 0] and [MATH: 1,] a [MATH: [100(1-\alpha)]\%] confidence interval for [MATH: p] is given by

Content:
[MATH: \widehat{\,p} \pm z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \sqrt{\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})}{n}}.]

Content:
where

Content:
- [MATH: z_{\alpha/2}] is the [MATH: z]-score satisfying [MATH: P(Z > z_{\alpha/2}) =\dfrac\alpha2,] and [MATH: Z\sim N(0,1),]
- [MATH: E = z_{\alpha/2}\cdot \sqrt{\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})}{n}}] is the margin of error.

Content:
These results assume that the sample elements are independent (i.e., the population we're drawing from is infinite). However, if the population size [MATH: N] is finite and not large compared to the sample size, the independence assumption is no longer valid.

Content:
In such cases, we can apply the finite population correction factor as follows:

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{\widehat{\,p} - p}{\sqrt{\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})}{n}\cdot \dfrac{N-n}{N-1}}\phantom{|}} \sim N(0,1).]

Content:
Then, the expression for our confidence interval is given by
[MATH: \widehat{\,p} \pm z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \sqrt{\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})}{n} \cdot \dfrac{N-n}{N-1}}.]

sections.normalized_html:
Consider a sample of size [MATH: n=65] from a population of size [MATH: N=310] where some individuals have a particular characteristic. Given that the proportion of those in the sample with the characteristic is [MATH: \widehat{\,p}=0.8,] find a [MATH: 90\%] confidence interval for the population proportion [MATH: p] of individuals having this characteristic.

Hint: Use the fact that [MATH: P(Z > 1.645) = 0.05,] where [MATH: Z \sim N(0,1),] as shown in the diagram above.
sections.readable_text:
Consider a sample of size [MATH: n=65] from a population of size [MATH: N=310] where some individuals have a particular characteristic. Given that the proportion of those in the sample with the characteristic is [MATH: \widehat{\,p}=0.8,] find a [MATH: 90\%] confidence interval for the population proportion [MATH: p] of individuals having this characteristic.

Hint: Use the fact that [MATH: P(Z > 1.645) = 0.05,] where [MATH: Z \sim N(0,1),] as shown in the diagram above.

[IMG: /graphics/f0adea85620219885f014ef59798a09f]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Since [MATH: n=65,] [MATH: N=310,] and [MATH: \widehat{\,p}=0.8,] we have that

  • [MATH: n \widehat{\,p} = 65 \cdot 0.8 = 52 > 5,]

  • [MATH: n(1-\widehat{\,p}) = 65 \cdot (1-0.8) = 13 > 5.]

As a result, we may use a normal approximation: [MATH: \dfrac{\widehat{\,p} - p}{\sqrt{\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})}{n}\cdot \dfrac{N-n}{N-1}}\phantom{|}} \sim N(0,1),]

where

  • [MATH: \!\widehat{\,p}] is the sample proportion,

  • [MATH: p] is the population proportion,

  • [MATH: n] is the sample size,

  • [MATH: N] is the population size.

Notice that the finite population correction factor [MATH: \dfrac{N-n}{N-1}] is necessary when the sample size is a significant proportion of the population, typically exceeding [MATH: 5\%\cdot N.] In our case, we have [MATH: 65 > 5\%\cdot N = 5\%\cdot 310 = 15.5.]

Then, given a value [MATH: \alpha] between [MATH: 0] and [MATH: 1,] the corresponding [MATH: [100(1-\alpha)]\%] confidence interval for the population proportion [MATH: p] of the original distribution can be written as [MATH: \widehat{\,p} \pm z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \sqrt{\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})}{n} \cdot \dfrac{N-n}{N-1}},] where [MATH: P(Z > z_{\alpha/2}) = \dfrac{\alpha}{2}] and [MATH: Z \sim N(0,1).]

We are interested in finding a [MATH: 90\%] confidence interval. So, we have [MATH: \alpha=1-0.9=0.1 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \dfrac{\alpha}{2}=0.05.]

We are given that [MATH: P(Z > 1.645) = 0.05.] As a result, [MATH: z_{\alpha/2} = z_{0.05} = 1.645.]

Therefore, a [MATH: 90\%] confidence interval for the population proportion [MATH: p] is

[MATH: 0.8 ± 1.645 ⋅ sqrt((0.8(1 − 0.8))/(65) ⋅ (310 − 65)/(310 − 1)),] which simplifies to [MATH: 0.8 ± 0.073.]

sections.readable_text:
A total of [MATH: N=400] students use an e-learning platform. In a random sample of [MATH: n=130] of these students, [MATH: 78] declared they were satisfied with the quality of the course materials.

Find a [MATH: 90\%] confidence interval for the population proportion [MATH: p] of students satisfied with the course materials.

Hint: Given a random variable [MATH: Z \sim N(0,1),] the table below shows the [MATH: z]-scores [MATH: z_p] such that [MATH: P(Z > z_p) = p] for some particular values of [MATH: p.]

| [MATH: p] | [MATH: 0.100] | [MATH: 0.050] | [MATH: 0.025] | [MATH: 0.010] | [MATH: 0.005] |
| [MATH: z_p] | [MATH: 1.282] | [MATH: 1.645] | [MATH: 1.960] | [MATH: 2.326] | [MATH: 2.576] |

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, let's interpret the data:

  • the population consists of all students subscribed to the e-learning platform,

  • some of the students are satisfied with the quality of the course materials, some aren't,

  • the size of the random sample is [MATH: n=130,]

  • the size of the population is [MATH: N=400,] and

  • the proportion of students from the sample who are satisfied can be found as follows: [MATH: \widehat{p\,} = \dfrac{78}{130} = 0.6]

Now, we have that [MATH: n=130,] [MATH: N=400,] and [MATH: \widehat{\,p}=0.6,] so

  • [MATH: n \widehat{\,p} = 130\cdot 0.6= 78> 5,]

  • [MATH: n(1-\widehat{\,p}) = 130\cdot (1-0.6) = 52> 5.]

As a result, we may use a normal approximation:

[MATH: \dfrac{\widehat{\,p} - p}{\sqrt{\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})}{n}\cdot \dfrac{N-n}{N-1}}\phantom{|}} \sim N(0,1),]

where

  • [MATH: \!\widehat{\,p}] is the sample proportion,

  • [MATH: p] is the population proportion,

  • [MATH: n] is the sample size,

  • [MATH: N] is the population size.

Notice that the finite population correction factor [MATH: \dfrac{N-n}{N-1}] is necessary when the sample size is a significant proportion of the population, typically exceeding [MATH: 5\%\cdot N.] In our case, we have

[MATH: 130> 5\%\cdot N = 5\%\cdot 400 = 20.]

Then, given a value [MATH: \alpha] between [MATH: 0] and [MATH: 1,] the corresponding [MATH: [100(1-\alpha)]\%] confidence interval for the population proportion [MATH: p] of the original distribution can be written as

[MATH: \widehat{\,p} \pm z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \sqrt{\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})}{n} \cdot \dfrac{N-n}{N-1}},]

where [MATH: P(Z > z_{\alpha/2}) = \dfrac{\alpha}{2}] and [MATH: Z \sim N(0,1).]

We are interested in finding a [MATH: 90\%] confidence interval. So, we have

[MATH: \alpha=1-0.9=0.1 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \dfrac{\alpha}{2}=0.05.]

We also need to find the [MATH: z]-score value [MATH: z_{0.05}] such that [MATH: P(Z > z_{0.05}) = 0.05,] where [MATH: Z \sim N(0,1).]

From the percentage points table of the normal distribution, we obtain that [MATH: z_{0.05}=1.645{:}]

[MATH: p]

[MATH: 0.100]

[MATH: \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}0.050}]

[MATH: 0.025]

[MATH: 0.010]

[MATH: 0.005]

[MATH: z_p]

[MATH: 1.282]

[MATH: \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}1.645}]

[MATH: 1.960]

[MATH: 2.326]

[MATH: 2.576]

Therefore, a [MATH: 90\%] confidence interval for the population proportion [MATH: p] is

[MATH: 0.6 ± 1.645 ⋅ sqrt((0.6(1 − 0.6))/(130) ⋅ (400 − 130)/(400 − 1)),]

which simplifies to

[MATH: 0.6 ± 0.058.]

Finally, [MATH: (0.6- 0.058, \, 0.6+ 0.058) = (0.54, 0.66).]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
In this lesson, we'll learn how to construct confidence intervals for population proportions when the population we're sampling is finite. First, let's quickly recap some important results.

Content:
Suppose we have a random sample of size [MATH: n] from a sufficiently large population where a proportion [MATH: p] of the population has a particular characteristic. Then, we have the following approximation:

Content:
[MATH: \widehat{\,p} \sim N\left(p, \dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}\right)]
where [MATH: \widehat{\,p}] is the sample proportion. Now, if we [MATH: z]-score this result, we have

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{\widehat{\,p} - p}{\sqrt{\dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}}} \sim N(0,1).]

Content:
Replacing our expression for the variance with its sample-based estimate, we have

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{\widehat{\,p} - p}{\sqrt{\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})}{n}}\phantom{|}} \sim N(0,1).]

Content:
For this result to be valid, the following conditions must be satisfied:

Content:
- More than five members of the sample have the characteristic [MATH: (n \widehat{\,p} > 5),] and
- More than five members of the sample do not have the characteristic [MATH: (n (1-\widehat{\,p}) > 5).]

Content:
Then, for a given value [MATH: \alpha] between [MATH: 0] and [MATH: 1,] a [MATH: [100(1-\alpha)]\%] confidence interval for [MATH: p] is given by

Content:
[MATH: \widehat{\,p} \pm z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \sqrt{\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})}{n}}.]

Content:
where

Content:
- [MATH: z_{\alpha/2}] is the [MATH: z]-score satisfying [MATH: P(Z > z_{\alpha/2}) =\dfrac\alpha2,] and [MATH: Z\sim N(0,1),]
- [MATH: E = z_{\alpha/2}\cdot \sqrt{\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})}{n}}] is the margin of error.

Content:
These results assume that the sample elements are independent (i.e., the population we're drawing from is infinite). However, if the population size [MATH: N] is finite and not large compared to the sample size, the independence assumption is no longer valid.

Content:
In such cases, we can apply the finite population correction factor as follows:

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{\widehat{\,p} - p}{\sqrt{\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})}{n}\cdot \dfrac{N-n}{N-1}}\phantom{|}} \sim N(0,1).]

Content:
Then, the expression for our confidence interval is given by
[MATH: \widehat{\,p} \pm z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \sqrt{\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})}{n} \cdot \dfrac{N-n}{N-1}}.]

---

Item 2 — Example: Finding Confidence Intervals for Population Proportions

Example Prompt:
Consider a sample of size [MATH: n=65] from a population of size [MATH: N=310] where some individuals have a particular characteristic. Given that the proportion of those in the sample with the characteristic is [MATH: \widehat{\,p}=0.8,] find a [MATH: 90\%] confidence interval for the population proportion [MATH: p] of individuals having this characteristic.

Hint: Use the fact that [MATH: P(Z > 1.645) = 0.05,] where [MATH: Z \sim N(0,1),] as shown in the diagram above.

[IMG: /graphics/f0adea85620219885f014ef59798a09f]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Since [MATH: n=65,] [MATH: N=310,] and [MATH: \widehat{\,p}=0.8,] we have that

- [MATH: n \widehat{\,p} = 65 \cdot 0.8 = 52 > 5,]
- [MATH: n(1-\widehat{\,p}) = 65 \cdot (1-0.8) = 13 > 5.]

As a result, we may use a normal approximation:
[MATH: \dfrac{\widehat{\,p} - p}{\sqrt{\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})}{n}\cdot \dfrac{N-n}{N-1}}\phantom{|}} \sim N(0,1),]

where

- [MATH: \!\widehat{\,p}] is the sample proportion,
- [MATH: p] is the population proportion,
- [MATH: n] is the sample size,
- [MATH: N] is the population size.

Notice that the finite population correction factor
[MATH: \dfrac{N-n}{N-1}]
is necessary when the sample size is a significant proportion of the population, typically exceeding [MATH: 5\%\cdot N.] In our case, we have
[MATH: 65 > 5\%\cdot N = 5\%\cdot 310 = 15.5.]

Then, given a value [MATH: \alpha] between [MATH: 0] and [MATH: 1,] the corresponding [MATH: [100(1-\alpha)]\%] confidence interval for the population proportion [MATH: p] of the original distribution can be written as
[MATH: \widehat{\,p} \pm z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \sqrt{\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})}{n} \cdot \dfrac{N-n}{N-1}},]
where [MATH: P(Z > z_{\alpha/2}) = \dfrac{\alpha}{2}] and [MATH: Z \sim N(0,1).]

We are interested in finding a [MATH: 90\%] confidence interval. So, we have
[MATH: \alpha=1-0.9=0.1 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\dfrac{\alpha}{2}=0.05.]

We are given that [MATH: P(Z > 1.645) = 0.05.] As a result,

[MATH: 0.8 ± 1.645 ⋅ sqrt((0.8(1 − 0.8))/(65) ⋅ (310 − 65)/(310 − 1)),]
which simplifies to
[MATH: 0.8 ± 0.073.]
